newsitem.title: ISRAEL: At least four killed in Tel Aviv bombing.
newsitem.headline: At least four killed in Tel Aviv bombing.

text.p: A bomb ripped through a crowded sidewalk cafe in Tel Aviv on Friday, killing at least four people in what Israeli police said was an apparent Moslem suicide attack.
The blast, which came amid heightened Israeli-Palestinian tension over the groundbreaking this week on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, injured 43 people, police said.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned the blast as a "terrorist incident". But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arafat's Palestinian Authority of indirectly giving a green light to those responsible for the attack.

"I said these organisations understood from the things that were said to them they had the approval of the Palestinian Authority...There is no doubt they acted on the basis of that understanding," Netanyahu told reporters at a hospital where wounded were being treated.
Israeli government spokesman Moshe Fogel said the attack could derail the Middle East peace process. "It is clearly going to hurt the peace process, if not derail it totally," Fogel told the BBC.

Police said said the four dead included the suspected bomber, who was carrying an Arab identity card. An anonymous telephone caller told police that the Islamic fundamentalist Hamas group carried out the attack.
"It was a terribly big explosion, the windows shattered to pieces," said Iris Gan, a waitress at the Apropos cafe on Tel Aviv's central Ben Gurion Street.
"I saw a woman lying on the ground covered with blood, being dragged to the ambulance," she said amid a throng of dazed survivors.
"There was a terrorist who blew himself up, apparently, a bomb, not very big," Police Commissioner Assaf Hefetz told reporters.
A witness told police that he saw a man at the cafe, which was crowded ahead of the Jewish Sabbath holiday, with a suspicious bag.
Israeli security forces had been on high alert in Jerusalem to prevent unrest after Friday's Moslem prayers by Palestinians opposed to his building a Jewish settlement on the outskirts of the city.
Israel imposed a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the attack.
In Gaza, Palestinian police prevented a scheduled rally by Hamas after news of the attack. Hamas claimed responsiblity for a wave of suicide attacks last year that killed 59 people in Israel.
In Helsinki, a senior White House official condemned the bombing and said U.S. President Bill Clinton, attending a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, would speak out against the attack.

"We're all saddened to learn of this explosion in Tel Aviv," the official said. "We all know that the way to make progress is not through violence, but through working together and our thoughts are now with the victims of this terrible act and their families."
A radical Palestinian group said Netanyahu should expect more attacks by Palestinians because he was rejecting peace with Arabs.

"As long as there is occupation and (Jewish) settlements over Arab lands, Netanyahu should expect Palestinians to defend themselves with all means and to launch more confrontations," Maher al-Taher, spokesman for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, said in Damascus.

Earlier on Friday in the West Bank town of Hebron, Israeli troops confronted Palestinian protesters across the line between Palestinian and Israeli-controlled areas in the worst unrest since Israel handed most of town to the Palestinians in January, witnesses said.

The army declared a curfew on the Israeli-controlled section where 400 Jewish settlers guarded by the army live among thousands of Palestinians. An army spokesman said the curfew forbade Palestinians, not Israelis, from moving around in the area.

Palestinians said at least 13 youths were lightly injured by rubber bullets and dozens were treated for teargas inhalation. Sirens wailed through the centre of Hebron as ambulances and police vans ferried the wounded to hospital.
